'''Joseph Andrew Johnson III''' (1940 – 2017) was an American physicist and professor at the [[Florida A&M University]]. He was a founding member of the [[National Society of Black Physicists]]. He was awarded the 1995 [[American Physical Society]] [[Edward Bouchet]] award and the 2016 [[Yale University]] Bouchet Leadership Award Medal.

== Early life and education ==
Johnson was born in [[Nashville, Tennessee]] to Grace and Bishop [[Joseph A. Johnson Jr.]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Johnson-Oliver|first=Cynthia|title=In Memoriam: Dr. Joseph A. Johnson III (1940-2017) {{!}} Bishop Joseph Johnson History Project|url=https://bishopjosephjohnson.org/2017/06/28/in-memoriam-dr-joseph-a-johnson-iii-1940-2017/|access-date=2021-02-22|language=en-US}}</ref> He attended [[Fisk University]] for his undergraduate studies, where he studied physics and graduated ''[[summa cum laude]]''.<ref name=":0" /> He moved to [[Yale University]] for his graduate studies, where he earned a master's in 1961 and PhD in 1965.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2016-04-14|title=Bouchet Medalists stress importance of diversity in science, universities|url=https://som.yale.edu/bouchet-medalists-stress-importance-diversity-science-universities|access-date=2021-02-22|website=Yale School of Management|language=en}}</ref> Johnson was the second African American to obtain a Ph.D. in physics from Yale.<ref name="Yale Memoriam"/> His research considered plasma dynamics and the production of pions in antiproton-proton collisions.<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Pion Production and Elastic Scattering in Antiproton-Proton Collisions at 7 BEV/C.|date=1965|place=New Haven, CT|language=English|first=Joseph Andrew III|last=Johnson|oclc=702765769}}</ref> He worked under the supervision of [[Henry Kraybill]].<ref name="Yale Memoriam">{{Cite web|title=Joseph Johnson III - in memoriam {{!}} Department of Physics|url=https://physics.yale.edu/news/joseph-johnson-iii-memoriam|access-date=2021-02-22|website=physics.yale.edu}}</ref> After graduating, Johnson worked at the [[Sikorsky Aircraft]] company and [[Bell Labs]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Joseph Johnson III|journal=Physics Today|year=2018|issue=5 |url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/do/10.1063/PT.6.6.20180526a/full/|language=en|doi=10.1063/PT.6.6.20180526a|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
Johnson was made Herbert Kayser Professor of Science and Engineering at the [[City College of New York]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Joseph Andrew Johnson III|url=https://ebasi.org/Johnson1_20170918072102/|access-date=2021-02-22|website=ebasi.org|language=en}}</ref> His research considered turbulence in plasmas and [[laser-induced fluorescence]].<ref name=":1" /> Johnson studied both fully turbulent collisional plasmas and magnetised turbulent plasmas.<ref name=":1" /> He was eventually appointed distinguished professor of science and engineering at [[Florida A&M University]], where he served as director of the Centre for Plasma Science.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|date=2016-04-14|title=Bouchet Medalists stress importance of diversity in science, universities|url=https://news.yale.edu/2016/04/14/bouchet-medalists-stress-importance-diversity-science-universities|access-date=2021-02-22|website=YaleNews|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite Q|Q105635629}}</ref>

Throughout his career, Johnson looked to support minority scientists and engineers. He was involved with outreach and education programmes for minority students, and supervised several doctoral researchers. In the early 1970s he helped to arrange the first meeting of African-American physicists.<ref name=":1" /> The meeting, which was hosted at [[Fisk University]], honoured [[Donald Anderson Edwards]], John Hunter and [[Halston Eagleson]].<ref name=":1" /> In 1977 Johnson was one of the founding members of the [[National Society of Black Physicists]] (NSBP). He helped to draft the constitution and went on to serve as President.<ref name=":1" /> His legacy is recognised by the [[American Institute of Physics]] and NSBP, who, in 2021, established the Joseph A. Johnson III Award for Excellence.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Howard University professor to receive first Joseph A. Johnson Award|url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2021-01/aiop-hup011521.php|access-date=2021-02-22|website=EurekAlert!|language=en}}</ref> In 1988 he worked with [[Abdus Salam]] to host a meeting for African and African-American physicists at the [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]].<ref name=":1" /> A direct outcome of the meeting was the formation of the [[Edward Bouchet Abdus Salam Institute]], which supports African doctoral researchers in attending graduate school in the [[United States]].<ref name=":1" /> In 2003 he helped to establish the African Laser Centre, a network of laser laboratories across Africa that provides fellowships for graduate students.<ref name=":1" />

== Awards and honors ==

* 1989 Elected Associate Fellow of the [[American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics]]<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=2021 Edward A. Bouchet Award Recipient|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/bouchet.cfm|access-date=2021-02-22|website=www.aps.org|language=en}}</ref>
* 1990 Elected Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]]<ref name=":3" />
* 1992 Charter Fellow of the National Society of Black Physicists<ref name=":3" />
* 1995 [[American Physical Society]] [[Edward Bouchet]] Award<ref name=":3" /> 
* 2016 [[Yale University]] Bouchet Leadership Award Medal<ref name=":2" />

== Personal life ==
Johnson was married to Lynette E. Johnson.<ref name=":0" /> Together they had four children and nine grandchildren.<ref name=":0" />
